sections.title: Section A — Units I to IV (compulsory)
Section B1 — Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
Section B2 — Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Commission on profit after salary but before commission
questions.question: A firm's profit before partners' salary and commission is ₹1,60,000. Partner Rekha gets a salary of ₹10,000. Partner Sohan gets a commission of 8% of the net profit after charging Rekha's salary but BEFORE charging his commission. Sohan's commission is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹12,000
Step 1: Profit after salary = ₹1,60,000 − ₹10,000 = ₹1,50,000
Step 2: Commission is 'before charging such commission', so a simple percentage applies: 8% × ₹1,50,000 = ₹12,000
Common mistake: Ignoring the salary gives ₹12,800 (A). Using the 'after commission' formula (8/108) on ₹1,50,000 gives ₹11,111 (B), and on ₹1,60,000 gives ₹11,852 (C).
Key point: 'Before commission' → simple %; 'after commission' → rate ÷ (100 + rate).

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Interest on capital — firm started during the year
questions.question: Pooja and Ravi started their firm on 1 August 2025. Pooja contributed capital of ₹1,50,000 on that date. The deed allows interest on capital at 9% p.a., and the books close on 31 March 2026. Pooja's interest on capital is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹9,000
Step 1: Period from 1 August 2025 to 31 March 2026 = 8 months
Step 2: Interest = ₹1,50,000 × 9% × 8/12 = ₹9,000
Common mistake: Charging a full year gives ₹13,500 (B). Using 6 months gives ₹6,750 (C). Using 10 months gives ₹11,250 (D).

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Interest on capital — additions and withdrawals during the year
questions.question: Dinesh's capital on 1 April 2025 was ₹2,00,000. He introduced ₹40,000 on 1 July 2025 and withdrew ₹30,000 from capital on 1 January 2026. Interest on capital is allowed at 10% p.a., and the books close on 31 March 2026. His interest on capital is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹22,250
Step 1: On the opening capital for 12 months = ₹2,00,000 × 10% = ₹20,000
Step 2: Add on the addition for 9 months (1 July–31 March) = ₹40,000 × 10% × 9/12 = ₹3,000
Step 3: Less on the withdrawal for 3 months (1 January–31 March) = ₹30,000 × 10% × 3/12 = ₹750
Step 4: Total = 20,000 + 3,000 − 750 = ₹22,250
Common mistake: Ignoring the withdrawal gives ₹23,000 (A). Ignoring the addition gives ₹19,250 (C). Using the net capital of ₹2,10,000 for a full year gives ₹21,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Legal limits in the issue of shares
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Item)
(A) Minimum subscription
(B) Minimum application money
(C) Interest on calls in arrears under Table F
(D) Interest on calls in advance under Table F

List-II (Limit)
(I) 90% of the issue
(II) 5% of the nominal value of the security
(III) Not more than 10% p.a.
(IV) Not more than 12% p.a.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(I), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)
Why:
(A) SEBI requires at least 90% of the issue to be subscribed (I).
(B) Section 39(2) requires application money of at least 5% of nominal value (II).
(C) Table F caps interest on calls in arrears at 10% p.a. (III).
(D) Table F caps interest on calls in advance at 12% p.a. (IV).
Why not the others: (A) swaps the two minimums; (C) swaps the two interest rates; (D) swaps minimum subscription and interest on advance.
Key point: Arrears 10%, advance 12%.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Share Forfeiture balance after part re-issue
questions.question: A company forfeited 500 shares on which ₹4 per share had been received, crediting ₹2,000 to the Share Forfeiture Account. It re-issued 300 of these shares at a discount of ₹1 per share and transferred the surplus on them to Capital Reserve. The balance remaining in the Share Forfeiture Account is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹800
Step 1: Discount on re-issue debited to Share Forfeiture = 300 × ₹1 = ₹300
Step 2: Surplus on the 300 re-issued shares = 300 × ₹4 − ₹300 = ₹900 → Capital Reserve
Step 3: Balance = ₹2,000 − ₹300 − ₹900 = ₹800, which relates to the 200 shares not re-issued (200 × ₹4)
Common mistake: ₹900 (A) is the Capital Reserve. Deducting only the transfer to Capital Reserve gives ₹1,100 (B). ₹2,000 (D) is the original balance.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Past adjustments — wrong ratio and omitted interest on capital
questions.question: Asha and Bhanu's profit of ₹60,000 for 2025-26 was distributed equally. However, the deed provides for profit sharing in the ratio 2 : 1 and for interest on capital at 5% p.a. on their fixed capitals of ₹1,00,000 and ₹50,000, which was not allowed. The single adjusting entry is:
options: A) Bhanu's Current A/c Dr. ₹10,000; To Asha's Current A/c ₹10,000
B) Asha's Current A/c Dr. ₹10,000; To Bhanu's Current A/c ₹10,000
C) Bhanu's Current A/c Dr. ₹1,250; To Asha's Current A/c ₹1,250
D) Bhanu's Current A/c Dr. ₹20,000; To Asha's Current A/c ₹20,000
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Bhanu's Current A/c Dr. ₹10,000; To Asha's Current A/c ₹10,000
Step 1: Correct distribution: interest on capital Asha ₹5,000, Bhanu ₹2,500; balance ₹52,500 shared 2 : 1 → Asha ₹35,000, Bhanu ₹17,500
Step 2: Correct totals: Asha ₹40,000; Bhanu ₹20,000
Step 3: Amounts actually credited: ₹30,000 each
Step 4: Asha is short by ₹10,000; Bhanu received ₹10,000 too much
Common mistake: Reversing the entry gives (B). Correcting only the omitted interest (keeping equal sharing) gives ₹1,250 (C). ₹20,000 (D) is the gap between their correct totals, not the adjustment.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Number of debentures from the total loss on issue
questions.question: A company issued 9% debentures of ₹100 each at a discount of 6%, redeemable at a premium of 4%. The total Loss on Issue of Debentures recorded was ₹30,000. The number of debentures issued is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 3,000
Step 1: Loss per debenture = Discount ₹6 + Premium on redemption ₹4 = ₹10
Step 2: Number = ₹30,000 ÷ ₹10 = 3,000
Common mistake: Using only the discount gives 5,000 (B). Using only the premium gives 7,500 (C). Doubling the loss per debenture gives 1,500 (D).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Retirement — retiring partner's share of revaluation profit
questions.question: Ashok, Bela and Chand share profits in the ratio 3 : 2 : 1. Chand retires. Land of ₹2,00,000 is appreciated by 25%; machinery of ₹60,000 is reduced to ₹54,000; bad debts of ₹3,000 are written off; and a liability of ₹8,000 for damages is to be created. Chand's share of the revaluation profit is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹5,500
Step 1: Gain on land = 25% × ₹2,00,000 = ₹50,000
Step 2: Losses = machinery ₹6,000 + bad debts ₹3,000 + damages ₹8,000 = ₹17,000
Step 3: Revaluation profit = ₹33,000 → Chand's share (1/6) = ₹5,500
Common mistake: Using Bela's 2/6 share gives ₹11,000 (B). Dividing by 4 gives ₹8,250 (C). Ignoring the liability for damages gives ₹6,833 (D).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Subscribed capital — meaning
questions.question: Subscribed capital is that part of the issued capital which:
options: A) Has been called up by the company
B) Has been paid up by the shareholders
C) Has been applied for by the public and allotted
D) Is authorised by the Memorandum of Association
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Has been applied for by the public and allotted
Why: Issued capital is what is offered; the part actually taken up (applied for and allotted) is subscribed capital.
Why not the others:
(A) Called-up capital is the part demanded.
(B) Paid-up capital is the part received.
(D) Authorised capital is the ceiling.
Key point: Offered → issued; taken → subscribed; demanded → called up; received → paid up.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Partner's salary as an appropriation in a loss year
questions.question:
Assertion (A): A salary payable to a partner under the deed, treated as an appropriation, is not allowed in a year in which the firm suffers a loss.
Reason (R): Appropriations are made only out of profits.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false
D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
Why: A partner's salary is normally an appropriation, debited to the P&L Appropriation Account. Since appropriations distribute profit (R), there is nothing to appropriate in a loss year, so the salary is not allowed (A).
Why not the others: (B) The Reason explains the Assertion. (C) and (D) Both statements are true.
Key point: Unless the deed makes it a charge, a partner's salary is paid only from profits.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Retirement — a continuing partner who sacrifices
questions.question: Ajit, Balu and Chirag share profits in the ratio 4 : 3 : 2. Chirag retires, and Ajit and Balu agree to share future profits in the ratio 1 : 2. Which statement about the adjustment of Chirag's share of goodwill is correct?
options: A) Ajit and Balu both gain and compensate Chirag in the ratio 1 : 2
B) Only Balu gains; he compensates both Chirag and Ajit
C) Ajit gains and compensates Chirag alone
D) No goodwill adjustment is needed
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Only Balu gains; he compensates both Chirag and Ajit
Step 1: Ajit: new 1/3 = 3/9; old 4/9 → change −1/9 (Ajit SACRIFICES)
Step 2: Balu: new 2/3 = 6/9; old 3/9 → gain 3/9
Step 3: Balu's gain (3/9) = Chirag's share (2/9) + Ajit's sacrifice (1/9), so Balu compensates both
Common mistake: Using the new ratio as the gaining ratio gives (A). (C) reverses Ajit's position. (D) ignores the change in shares.
Key point: On retirement, a continuing partner can also sacrifice — always compute each change.

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Dissolution by notice — partnership at will
questions.question: Under Section 43 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, a firm may be dissolved by any partner giving notice in writing to all the others. This applies to:
options: A) A partnership for a fixed term
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) A partnership at will
Why: A partnership at will has no fixed period or specific undertaking, so any partner may end it by written notice, effective from the date mentioned in the notice.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) continue until the term ends or the venture is completed, unless the partners agree otherwise. (C) Notice is not available to every firm.
Key point: Partnership at will → dissolution by notice (Section 43).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Admission — premium when goodwill is valued on average profit
questions.question: Goodwill of ₹40,000 already appears in the books of Arya and Bina, and it is to be written off. The firm's goodwill is now valued at two years' purchase of the average profit of ₹60,000. Charu is admitted for a 1/4th share. The premium for goodwill Charu must bring is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹30,000
Step 1: Goodwill of the firm = ₹60,000 × 2 = ₹1,20,000
Step 2: Charu's share = ₹1,20,000 × 1/4 = ₹30,000
Step 3: The existing goodwill of ₹40,000 is written off separately among the OLD partners; it does not reduce the premium
Common mistake: Netting the book goodwill (1/4 × ₹80,000) gives ₹20,000 (A). ₹1,20,000 (B) is the firm's goodwill. 1/4 of the book goodwill gives ₹10,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Accounts credited in reconstitution entries
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Item)
(A) Profit on revaluation at the time of admission
(B) Premium for goodwill brought in cash by the new partner
(C) Retiring partner's share of goodwill
(D) Final balance due to a deceased partner

List-II (Account credited)
(I) Old partners' Capital Accounts
(II) Premium for Goodwill Account
(III) Retiring partner's Capital Account
(IV) Executor's Account
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(I), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)
Why:
(A) Revaluation profit belongs to the old partners (I).
(B) Cash brought for goodwill is first credited to Premium for Goodwill (II) and then transferred to the sacrificing partners.
(C) The retiring partner is credited with his share of goodwill (III).
(D) The deceased partner's balance is transferred to his executor (IV).
Why not the others: (A) swaps revaluation profit and premium; (B) swaps premium and retiring partner; (C) swaps revaluation profit and executor.
Key point: Follow the money to the person who is entitled to it.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Hidden goodwill — meaning
questions.question:
Assertion (A): Hidden goodwill arises when the capital brought by a new partner implies a total value of the firm higher than the combined capitals of all the partners.
Reason (R): The excess of the implied value over the actual combined capital is treated as the firm's goodwill.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false
D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
Why: If a new partner pays ₹1,00,000 for a 1/4 share, the whole firm is implicitly worth ₹4,00,000. If the partners' combined capital (including his) is less than this, the difference represents value not recorded in the books — goodwill (R). That is why hidden goodwill exists (A).
Why not the others: (B) The Reason explains the Assertion. (C) and (D) Both statements are true.
Key point: Hidden goodwill = Implied total capital − Actual total capital.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Goodwill — working back to average profit
questions.question: A firm's capital employed is ₹3,00,000 and the normal rate of return is 10%. Its goodwill, valued at two years' purchase of super profit, is ₹40,000. The firm's average profit is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹50,000
Step 1: Super profit = ₹40,000 ÷ 2 = ₹20,000
Step 2: Normal profit = 10% × ₹3,00,000 = ₹30,000
Step 3: Average profit = Normal profit + Super profit = ₹50,000
Common mistake: ₹20,000 (B) is the super profit. ₹30,000 (C) is the normal profit. Adding the goodwill to normal profit gives ₹70,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Memorandum Revaluation Account — when used
questions.question: A Memorandum Revaluation Account is prepared on reconstitution when:
options: A) The firm is being dissolved
B) The partners want to record the effect of revaluation on their capitals without changing the book values of assets and liabilities
C) The new partner brings premium for goodwill in cash
D) A partner dies before the end of the year
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The partners want to record the effect of revaluation on their capitals without changing the book values of assets and liabilities
Why: The first part records the revaluation and divides the result in the OLD ratio; the second part reverses it in the NEW ratio. The net effect adjusts the capitals, while the assets and liabilities stay at their old values.
Why not the others: (A) Dissolution uses the Realisation Account. (C) and (D) do not by themselves require a memorandum account.
Key point: Memorandum Revaluation A/c = adjust capitals, keep book values.

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Section 48 — order of payments on dissolution
questions.question:
Arrange the following payments out of the realised assets of a dissolved firm in the order laid down by Section 48:
(A) Payment of the partners' capitals
(B) Payment of debts to outside creditors
(C) Repayment of partners' loans and advances
(D) Distribution of any surplus in the profit-sharing ratio
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (B), (C), (A), (D)
Why: Section 48(b) says the assets are applied first to pay debts to third parties (B), then each partner's advances as distinct from capital (C), then each partner's capital (A), and finally any residue is divided in the profit-sharing ratio (D).
Why not the others: (A) puts partners' loans before outsiders. (B) puts capital before loans. (D) puts capital first.
Key point: Outsiders → loans → capital → surplus.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Notes to accounts — share capital disclosures
questions.question:
Which of the following are disclosed in the notes to accounts relating to Share Capital?
(A) Authorised capital
(B) Issued capital
(C) Subscribed and fully paid, and subscribed but not fully paid capital
(D) The market price of the company's shares on the balance sheet date
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: Schedule III requires the notes to show authorised (A), issued (B) and subscribed capital split into fully paid and not fully paid (C), along with calls in arrears and forfeited shares.
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — the market price of shares is not part of the accounting disclosure of share capital, which is shown at face value. Options (A), (B) and (D) include it.
Key point: Share capital notes show face values, never market prices.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Fixed and fluctuating capitals — features
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about partners' capital accounts:
(A) Under the fluctuating capital method, only a Capital Account is kept for each partner.
(B) Under the fixed capital method, the Capital Account normally shows the same credit balance unless capital is added or withdrawn.
(C) Under the fluctuating capital method, a Capital Account may show a debit balance.
(D) Under the fixed capital method, interest on capital is credited to the Capital Account.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: With fluctuating capitals, all items go to one Capital Account (A), and heavy drawings or losses can make it debit (C). With fixed capitals, the Capital Account stays stable (B).
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — under the fixed capital method, interest on capital (like salary and profit share) is credited to the CURRENT Account. Options (A), (B) and (D) include it.
Key point: Fixed method → routine items in the Current A/c; fluctuating method → everything in the Capital A/c.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Debentures as collateral — second method entry
questions.question: A company issues 9% debentures as collateral security for a bank loan and decides to RECORD them in its books. The journal entry is:
options: A) Debenture Suspense A/c Dr.; To 9% Debentures A/c
B) Bank A/c Dr.; To 9% Debentures A/c
C) 9% Debentures A/c Dr.; To Bank Loan A/c
D) No entry can ever be passed for collateral debentures
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Debenture Suspense A/c Dr.; To 9% Debentures A/c
Why: Under the second method, the debentures are recorded, and the Debenture Suspense Account is shown on the assets side as a deduction from the debentures, so that no real liability is overstated.
Why not the others:
(B) No cash is received for collateral debentures.
(C) reverses the logic and confuses the loan with the debentures.
(D) Recording is optional, not prohibited.
Key point: Method 1 → note only; Method 2 → Debenture Suspense entry.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Registration of a firm — effect of non-registration
questions.question: Under Section 69 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, a partnership firm can file a suit against a third party in its own name to enforce a contract only if the firm is:
options: B) Formed under a written deed
D) Made up of more than ten partners
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Registered
Why: Registration is optional, but Section 69 bars an UNREGISTERED firm (and its partners) from suing third parties to enforce contractual rights. Third parties, however, can still sue an unregistered firm.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) are not conditions laid down by Section 69.
Key point: Registration is not compulsory, but it is necessary in practice to enforce the firm's rights.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Interest on calls in advance — accounting nature
questions.question: Interest paid by a company on calls received in advance is:
options: A) Credited to the Calls in Advance Account
B) Debited to the Share Capital Account
C) An appropriation of profit, like dividend
D) A finance cost, debited to Interest on Calls in Advance A/c and transferred to the Statement of Profit and Loss
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) A finance cost, debited to Interest on Calls in Advance A/c and transferred to the Statement of Profit and Loss
Why: The company is using the shareholder's money before it is due, so the interest is a cost of finance — payable even if there are no profits.
Why not the others:
(A) The advance itself is credited to Calls in Advance; the interest is a separate expense.
(B) Share capital is unaffected.
(C) Dividend is an appropriation; this interest is not.
Key point: Interest on calls in advance = finance cost; interest on calls in arrears = other income.

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Outside liabilities transferred to the Realisation Account
questions.question: On the dissolution of Arora & Co., the balance sheet shows: creditors ₹30,000; bills payable ₹10,000; a loan from Mrs Arora (wife of partner Arora) ₹20,000; Arora's own loan ₹15,000; and General Reserve ₹9,000. The total of liabilities transferred to the credit side of the Realisation Account is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹60,000
Step 1: Outside liabilities: creditors ₹30,000 + bills payable ₹10,000 + Mrs Arora's loan ₹20,000 = ₹60,000 (she is an outsider to the firm)
Step 2: Arora's own loan is paid directly, and General Reserve goes to the partners' capitals
Common mistake: Including Arora's loan gives ₹75,000 (A). Treating Mrs Arora's loan as a partner's loan gives ₹40,000 (C). Including the reserve gives ₹69,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Retirement — continuing partners bring cash to pay the retiring partner and fix capitals
questions.question: After all adjustments on Chetan's retirement, the capitals are: Amit ₹1,40,000, Bimal ₹1,10,000 and Chetan ₹70,000. The firm's cash balance is ₹30,000. Chetan is to be paid in full. Amit and Bimal will bring in enough cash to pay Chetan and leave a cash balance of ₹20,000, and their capitals are to be in their new profit-sharing ratio of 3 : 2. The cash Amit must bring in is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹46,000
Step 1: Cash needed = Payment to Chetan ₹70,000 + Minimum balance ₹20,000 − Existing cash ₹30,000 = ₹60,000
Step 2: Total capital of the new firm = ₹1,40,000 + ₹1,10,000 + ₹60,000 = ₹3,10,000
Step 3: Amit's required capital = ₹3,10,000 × 3/5 = ₹1,86,000 → he brings ₹1,86,000 − ₹1,40,000 = ₹46,000 (Bimal brings ₹14,000)
Common mistake: Ignoring the cash balance condition (total ₹3,00,000) gives ₹40,000 (A). Splitting the ₹60,000 in 3 : 2 gives ₹36,000 (C). ₹60,000 (D) is the total cash needed.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Admission — who decides the new ratio
questions.question: On the admission of a new partner, the new profit-sharing ratio is decided by:
options: D) Agreement among all the partners, including the new partner
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Agreement among all the partners, including the new partner
Why: Admission is a new agreement. Section 31 requires the consent of all existing partners to admit a new partner, and the terms, including the new ratio, are settled by agreement among all of them.
Why not the others: (A) Courts do not fix profit ratios. (B) and (C) No single partner can decide alone.
Key point: Admission = new agreement with everyone's consent.

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Accumulated profits and losses on dissolution
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the treatment of accumulated items on dissolution:
(A) A debit balance of the Profit and Loss Account is debited to the partners' Capital Accounts in their profit-sharing ratio.
(B) Deferred revenue expenditure, such as Advertisement Suspense, is written off to the partners' Capital Accounts.
(C) General Reserve is credited to the partners' Capital Accounts.
(D) Partners' Current Account balances are transferred to the Realisation Account.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: Accumulated losses (A) and fictitious assets (B) are written off against the partners, and accumulated profits (C) are credited to them, all in the profit-sharing ratio.
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — Current Account balances are transferred to the partners' Capital Accounts, not to the Realisation Account. Options (A), (C) and (D) include it.
Key point: Realisation A/c takes only assets and outside liabilities.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Goodwill — capital employed excludes fictitious and intangible items
questions.question: A firm's total assets of ₹5,30,000 include Goodwill of ₹20,000 and Advertisement Suspense of ₹10,000. Its outside liabilities are ₹1,00,000. Its average profit is ₹60,000 and the normal rate of return is 12%. By the capitalisation of average profit method, goodwill is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹1,00,000
Step 1: Capitalised value = ₹60,000 × 100/12 = ₹5,00,000
Step 2: Capital employed = 5,30,000 − 20,000 (goodwill) − 10,000 (advertisement suspense) − 1,00,000 = ₹4,00,000
Step 3: Goodwill = ₹5,00,000 − ₹4,00,000 = ₹1,00,000
Common mistake: Excluding neither item (₹4,30,000) gives ₹70,000 (A). Excluding only the suspense gives ₹80,000 (B). Excluding only the goodwill gives ₹90,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Admission — accumulated profits and deferred expenditure together
questions.question: Arpit and Bina share profits in the ratio 3 : 2. When Chirag is admitted, their balance sheet shows General Reserve ₹30,000, a credit balance of ₹12,000 in the Profit and Loss Account, and Advertisement Suspense (deferred revenue expenditure) of ₹6,000. The net amount credited to Arpit's Capital Account for these items is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹21,600
Step 1: Net accumulated profit = 30,000 + 12,000 − 6,000 = ₹36,000
Step 2: Arpit's share (3/5) = ₹21,600
Common mistake: Ignoring the Advertisement Suspense gives ₹25,200 (A). Taking only the General Reserve gives ₹18,000 (B). Adding the suspense instead of deducting it gives ₹28,800 (D).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Retirement — treatment of goodwill already in the books
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about goodwill on the retirement of a partner:
(A) Goodwill already appearing in the books is written off among ALL the partners in their old ratio.
(B) The retiring partner's share of goodwill is debited to the gaining partners.
(C) Goodwill is not raised in the books for this purpose.
(D) The retiring partner bears no part of the write-off of goodwill already in the books.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: Existing goodwill is written off in the old ratio, including the retiring partner (A). His share of the current value is then credited to him and debited to the gaining partners (B), without raising a Goodwill Account (C).
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — the retiring partner was an owner when that goodwill was recorded, so he bears his share of the write-off. Options (B), (C) and (D) include it.
Key point: Write off old goodwill (old ratio) → adjust the current value (gaining ratio).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Retirement — why goodwill is valued
questions.question: Goodwill is valued at the time of a partner's retirement mainly because the retiring partner:
options: A) Wants to join another firm
B) Helped build the firm's reputation and gives up his share of its future profits
C) Must pay the firm's outstanding liabilities
D) Receives a salary from the firm
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Helped build the firm's reputation and gives up his share of its future profits
Why: The continuing partners will enjoy the retiring partner's share of future (super) profits, which partly come from the goodwill he helped create. So he is compensated for his share of goodwill by the gaining partners.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) are not reasons for valuing goodwill.
Key point: Retirement → continuing partners gain → they compensate the retiring partner.

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Realisation with goodwill realised and partner's commission on realisation
questions.question: On dissolution, the firm's assets (other than cash) of ₹1,80,000, including Goodwill of ₹20,000, realised ₹1,80,000 in total (goodwill fetching ₹30,000). Creditors of ₹50,000 were paid ₹48,000 in full settlement. Partner Arun was allowed a commission of 2% on the total amount realised from assets, and realisation expenses of ₹2,000 were paid by the firm. The loss on realisation is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹3,600
Step 1: Debit side = assets 1,80,000 + creditors paid 48,000 + Arun's commission (2% × ₹1,80,000) 3,600 + expenses 2,000 = ₹2,33,600
Step 2: Credit side = creditors 50,000 + cash from assets 1,80,000 = ₹2,30,000
Step 3: Loss = ₹2,33,600 − ₹2,30,000 = ₹3,600
Common mistake: Ignoring the commission gives Nil (A). Ignoring the discount from creditors gives ₹5,600 (B). Ignoring the expenses gives ₹1,600 (C).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Re-issue of forfeited shares where premium had been received
questions.question: 600 shares of ₹10 each were issued at a premium of ₹3, payable ₹3 on application, ₹5 on allotment (₹2 capital + ₹3 premium) and ₹5 on the first and final call. Their holder paid the application and allotment money but not the call, and the shares were forfeited. Of these, 400 shares were re-issued at ₹8 per share as fully paid. The amount transferred to Capital Reserve is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹1,200
Step 1: Amount forfeited per share = capital paid = ₹3 + ₹2 = ₹5 (the ₹3 premium was RECEIVED, so it stays in Securities Premium)
Step 2: Discount on re-issue = ₹10 − ₹8 = ₹2 per share
Step 3: Capital Reserve = 400 × (₹5 − ₹2) = ₹1,200
Common mistake: ₹3,000 (A) is the total forfeited on 600 shares. Ignoring the discount gives ₹2,000 (B). Treating the premium as forfeited (₹8 per share) gives ₹2,400 (C).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Death — interest to the executor until payment
questions.question: The balance of ₹1,20,000 transferred to a deceased partner's Executor's Account is paid three months after the date of death, together with interest at 6% p.a. for the delay. The total amount paid to the executor is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹1,21,800
Step 1: Interest = ₹1,20,000 × 6% × 3/12 = ₹1,800
Step 2: Payment = ₹1,20,000 + ₹1,800 = ₹1,21,800
Common mistake: Charging interest for a full year gives ₹1,27,200 (A). Ignoring interest gives ₹1,20,000 (B). Using 6 months gives ₹1,23,600 (C).
Key point: Section 37 entitles the outgoing partner's representative to 6% p.a. interest (or a share of profit) until settlement.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Divisible profit after manager's commission, partner's salary and interest on drawings
questions.question: A firm's profit before the manager's commission is ₹1,10,000. The manager (an employee) is entitled to a commission of 10% of the net profit after charging his commission. The partners are entitled to salaries totalling ₹12,000, and interest on drawings of ₹2,000 is to be charged. The profit available for distribution in the profit-sharing ratio is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹90,000
Step 1: Manager's commission (a charge) = ₹1,10,000 × 10/110 = ₹10,000 → net profit ₹1,00,000
Step 2: Add interest on drawings ₹2,000; less partners' salaries ₹12,000
Step 3: Divisible profit = 1,00,000 + 2,000 − 12,000 = ₹90,000
Common mistake: ₹1,00,000 (A) stops after the commission. Deducting the interest on drawings instead of adding it gives ₹86,000 (B) — interest on drawings always ADDS to divisible profit. Taking the commission as 10% of ₹1,10,000 gives ₹89,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Under-subscription — application money received
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

Comet Ltd. invited applications for 50,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at a premium of ₹2 per share, payable as follows: ₹3 on application; ₹5 on allotment (including the premium); and ₹4 on the first and final call. Applications were received for 45,000 shares, which met the minimum subscription, and all applicants were allotted shares in full. Neha, who holds 500 shares, paid the call money along with her allotment money. The first and final call was made three months after allotment; Neha's advance was adjusted against it. Ravi, who holds 1,000 shares, did not pay the call money. The company has adopted Table F.

Question: The amount received on application is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹1,35,000
Step 1: Applications received = 45,000 shares
Step 2: Application money = 45,000 × ₹3 = ₹1,35,000
Common mistake: Using the 50,000 shares offered gives ₹1,50,000 (A). ₹1,80,000 (C) and ₹90,000 (D) use wrong rates or numbers.
Key point: Under-subscription → only the shares applied for are allotted.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Under-subscription — allotment money with calls in advance
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

Comet Ltd. invited applications for 50,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at a premium of ₹2 per share, payable as follows: ₹3 on application; ₹5 on allotment (including the premium); and ₹4 on the first and final call. Applications were received for 45,000 shares, which met the minimum subscription, and all applicants were allotted shares in full. Neha, who holds 500 shares, paid the call money along with her allotment money. The first and final call was made three months after allotment; Neha's advance was adjusted against it. Ravi, who holds 1,000 shares, did not pay the call money. The company has adopted Table F.

Question: The total amount received at the time of allotment (including any calls in advance) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹2,27,000
Step 1: Allotment money = 45,000 × ₹5 = ₹2,25,000
Step 2: Neha's call paid in advance = 500 × ₹4 = ₹2,000 (credited to Calls in Advance A/c)
Step 3: Total received = ₹2,27,000
Common mistake: Leaving out Neha's advance gives ₹2,25,000 (B). Leaving out the premium (45,000 × ₹3) gives ₹1,35,000 (C). Using 50,000 shares gives ₹2,50,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Call money received with arrears and advance
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

Comet Ltd. invited applications for 50,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at a premium of ₹2 per share, payable as follows: ₹3 on application; ₹5 on allotment (including the premium); and ₹4 on the first and final call. Applications were received for 45,000 shares, which met the minimum subscription, and all applicants were allotted shares in full. Neha, who holds 500 shares, paid the call money along with her allotment money. The first and final call was made three months after allotment; Neha's advance was adjusted against it. Ravi, who holds 1,000 shares, did not pay the call money. The company has adopted Table F.

Question: The cash received when the first and final call is made is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹1,74,000
Step 1: Call due = 45,000 × ₹4 = ₹1,80,000
Step 2: Less Ravi's unpaid call = 1,000 × ₹4 = ₹4,000 (calls in arrears)
Step 3: Less Neha's call already received in advance = 500 × ₹4 = ₹2,000
Step 4: Cash received now = 1,80,000 − 4,000 − 2,000 = ₹1,74,000
Common mistake: Ignoring both gives ₹1,80,000 (A). Ignoring the advance gives ₹1,76,000 (B). Ignoring the arrears gives ₹1,78,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Interest on calls in advance — Table F, for part of a year
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

Comet Ltd. invited applications for 50,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at a premium of ₹2 per share, payable as follows: ₹3 on application; ₹5 on allotment (including the premium); and ₹4 on the first and final call. Applications were received for 45,000 shares, which met the minimum subscription, and all applicants were allotted shares in full. Neha, who holds 500 shares, paid the call money along with her allotment money. The first and final call was made three months after allotment; Neha's advance was adjusted against it. Ravi, who holds 1,000 shares, did not pay the call money. The company has adopted Table F.

Question: The maximum interest payable to Neha on her calls in advance under Table F is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹60
Step 1: Advance = 500 × ₹4 = ₹2,000, held for 3 months (from allotment until the call)
Step 2: Table F allows interest on calls in advance at up to 12% p.a.
Step 3: Interest = ₹2,000 × 12% × 3/12 = ₹60
Common mistake: Using 10% (the arrears rate) gives ₹50 (A). A full year gives ₹240 (C). Six months gives ₹120 (D).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Share capital shown after under-subscription, arrears and advance
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

Comet Ltd. invited applications for 50,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at a premium of ₹2 per share, payable as follows: ₹3 on application; ₹5 on allotment (including the premium); and ₹4 on the first and final call. Applications were received for 45,000 shares, which met the minimum subscription, and all applicants were allotted shares in full. Neha, who holds 500 shares, paid the call money along with her allotment money. The first and final call was made three months after allotment; Neha's advance was adjusted against it. Ravi, who holds 1,000 shares, did not pay the call money. The company has adopted Table F.

Question: After the call, the amount of share capital shown in the balance sheet (subscribed capital less calls in arrears) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹4,46,000
Step 1: Subscribed and called-up capital = 45,000 × ₹10 = ₹4,50,000
Step 2: Less calls in arrears (Ravi) = ₹4,000 → ₹4,46,000
Step 3: Neha's advance was adjusted when the call was made, so no Calls in Advance balance remains
Common mistake: Ignoring arrears gives ₹4,50,000 (A). Using the 50,000 shares offered gives ₹5,00,000 (B). Also deducting Neha's advance gives ₹4,44,000 (C). The premium of ₹90,000 is shown separately under Securities Premium.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Trade payables turnover — cash purchases and bills payable
questions.question: Total purchases for the year are ₹6,00,000, of which ₹1,50,000 are cash purchases. Creditors were ₹35,000 at the start and ₹45,000 at the end of the year; bills payable were ₹5,000 at the start and ₹15,000 at the end. The trade payables turnover ratio is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 9 times
Step 1: Net credit purchases = ₹6,00,000 − ₹1,50,000 = ₹4,50,000
Step 2: Trade payables = creditors + bills payable: opening ₹40,000; closing ₹60,000 → average ₹50,000
Step 3: Turnover = ₹4,50,000 ÷ ₹50,000 = 9 times
Common mistake: Using total purchases gives 12 times (A). Leaving out bills payable gives 11.25 times (B). Using the closing balance gives 7.5 times (C).

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Trend analysis — meaning
questions.question: An analyst takes 2021-22 as the base year (= 100) and expresses each later year's revenue and profit as a percentage of the base year. This tool of analysis is called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Trend analysis
Why: Trend analysis converts the figures of several years into index numbers (percentages of a base year) to show the direction and pace of change.
Why not the others:
(A) Comparative statements usually compare two years with absolute and percentage changes.
(B) Common-size statements compare items within one year against a base such as revenue.
(D) Ratio analysis relates different items to each other.
Key point: Base year = 100 → trend percentages.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Schedule III — surplus in the statement of profit and loss
questions.question: As per Schedule III, the credit balance of the Statement of Profit and Loss (Surplus) is shown in the balance sheet under:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Reserves and surplus
Why: Undistributed profits belong to the shareholders, so the Surplus is part of Shareholders' funds under Reserves and surplus. (A debit balance is shown there as a negative figure.)
Why not the others:
(B) It is not owed to outsiders.
(C) Share capital is the amount contributed by shareholders.
(D) A credit balance is not an asset.
Key point: Surplus = retained profits → Reserves and surplus.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Gross profit ratio — cost of revenue from inventory, purchases and returns
questions.question: A trader's revenue from operations is ₹5,00,000. Opening inventory was ₹50,000, purchases ₹4,20,000, purchase returns ₹20,000 and closing inventory ₹70,000. The gross profit ratio is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 24%
Step 1: Net purchases = ₹4,20,000 − ₹20,000 = ₹4,00,000
Step 2: Cost of revenue = 50,000 + 4,00,000 − 70,000 = ₹3,80,000
Step 3: Gross profit = ₹1,20,000 → GP ratio = ₹1,20,000 ÷ ₹5,00,000 × 100 = 24%
Common mistake: Ignoring the returns gives 20% (B). 76% (C) is the cost ratio. Ignoring the closing inventory gives 10% (D).

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Cash flow statement — basic features
questions.question:
Which of the following statements about a cash flow statement are correct?
(A) It is prepared on a cash basis.
(B) Cash equivalents include short-term, highly liquid investments maturing within three months.
(C) Non-cash transactions are not shown in it.
(D) It replaces the Statement of Profit and Loss.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: AS 3 requires a statement of actual cash movements (A), treats near-cash investments with a maturity of three months or less as cash equivalents (B), and leaves out transactions that involve no cash (C).
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — the cash flow statement SUPPLEMENTS the Statement of Profit and Loss; profit (accrual basis) and cash flow measure different things. Options (A), (B) and (D) include it.
Key point: Profit ≠ cash; both statements are needed.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Cash flow from operating activities — non-operating items and tax
questions.question: A manufacturing company's net profit before tax of ₹2,40,000 includes a profit on sale of investments of ₹10,000 and dividend received of ₹8,000. Depreciation was ₹30,000 and goodwill of ₹12,000 was written off. Trade receivables increased by ₹20,000, trade payables decreased by ₹5,000, and income tax paid was ₹50,000. Net cash from operating activities is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹1,89,000
Step 1: Remove non-operating incomes: 2,40,000 − 10,000 − 8,000 = ₹2,22,000
Step 2: Add non-cash expenses: + 30,000 + 12,000 = ₹2,64,000
Step 3: Working capital: − 20,000 (receivables up) − 5,000 (payables down) = ₹2,39,000
Step 4: Less tax paid ₹50,000 = ₹1,89,000
Common mistake: Not removing the non-operating incomes gives ₹2,07,000 (A). Deducting the goodwill written off gives ₹1,65,000 (B). Stopping before tax gives ₹2,39,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Inventory turnover — cost worked out from a mark-up on cost
questions.question: A trader's revenue from operations is ₹4,80,000, and he earns a gross profit of 25% ON COST. Opening inventory is ₹40,000 and closing inventory ₹56,000. The inventory turnover ratio is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 8 times
Step 1: Gross profit is 25% on cost → revenue = 125% of cost → cost of revenue = ₹4,80,000 × 100/125 = ₹3,84,000
Step 2: Average inventory = (₹40,000 + ₹56,000) ÷ 2 = ₹48,000
Step 3: Inventory turnover = ₹3,84,000 ÷ ₹48,000 = 8 times
Common mistake: Using revenue gives 10 times (A). Using closing inventory gives 6.86 times (B). Using opening inventory gives 9.6 times (C).

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Cash flow from investing activities — partly non-cash purchase
questions.question: A company bought land for ₹3,00,000. It paid ₹1,00,000 of this by issuing equity shares to the seller and the balance in cash. The cash outflow shown under investing activities is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹2,00,000
Why: Only the cash paid is a cash flow. The part settled by issuing shares is a non-cash transaction and is excluded (though disclosed separately).
Step 1: Cash paid = ₹3,00,000 − ₹1,00,000 = ₹2,00,000 (investing outflow)
Common mistake: Taking the full price gives ₹3,00,000 (A). ₹1,00,000 (C) is the non-cash part. Nil (D) ignores the cash paid.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Effect of transactions on the current ratio
questions.question: A company's current ratio is 2 : 1. Which of the following transactions will NOT change it?
options: A) Collection of cash from debtors
B) Purchase of goods on credit
C) Payment of cash to creditors
D) Sale of a fixed asset for cash
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Collection of cash from debtors
Why: Cash rises and debtors fall by the same amount; both are current assets, so total current assets and current liabilities are unchanged.
Why not the others:
(B) Both sides rise by the same amount, which lowers a ratio that is above 1.
(C) Both sides fall, which raises a ratio above 1.
(D) Current assets rise with no change in liabilities.
Key point: An exchange of one current asset for another leaves the current ratio unchanged.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Schedule III — classification of items
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II as per Schedule III:

List-I (Item)
(A) Capital work-in-progress
(B) Calls in advance
(C) Provision for tax
(D) Bills payable

List-II (Sub-head)
(I) Property, Plant and Equipment and Intangible Assets
(II) Other current liabilities
(III) Short-term provisions
(IV) Trade payables
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(I), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)
Why:
(A) An asset under construction sits with PPE and Intangible Assets (I).
(B) Calls in advance are refundable amounts owed → other current liabilities (II).
(C) Provision for tax is an estimated liability → short-term provisions (III).
(D) Bills payable arise from purchases → trade payables (IV).
Why not the others: (A) swaps CWIP and calls in advance; (C) swaps calls in advance and provision; (D) swaps CWIP and bills payable.
Key point: Ask what the item is, and when it falls due.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Payroll — gross salary with several allowances
questions.question: An employee's basic pay is ₹22,000 and DA is 30% of basic pay. She also gets a conveyance allowance of ₹1,600 and a medical allowance of ₹1,250. Her gross salary in the payroll sheet is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹31,450
Step 1: DA = 30% × ₹22,000 = ₹6,600
Step 2: Gross = 22,000 + 6,600 + 1,600 + 1,250 = ₹31,450
Common mistake: Basic + DA only gives ₹28,600 (B). Leaving out the conveyance allowance gives ₹29,850 (C). Leaving out DA gives ₹24,850 (D).

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Payroll — professional tax slab with nested IF, then net salary
questions.question: A payroll sheet computes professional tax with =IF(B2>20000,200,IF(B2>15000,150,0)). An employee's gross salary in B2 is ₹18,000, and PF of 12% of gross is also deducted. Her net salary is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹15,690
Step 1: 18,000 > 20,000? FALSE → inner IF: 18,000 > 15,000? TRUE → professional tax = ₹150
Step 2: PF = 12% × ₹18,000 = ₹2,160
Step 3: Net = 18,000 − 150 − 2,160 = ₹15,690
Common mistake: Applying the top slab (₹200) gives ₹15,640 (B). Treating both tests as false (₹0) gives ₹15,840 (C). Ignoring PF gives ₹17,850 (D).

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Electronic spreadsheet — text functions
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Function)
(A) =UPPER
(B) =TRIM
(C) =CONCATENATE
(D) =PROPER

List-II (Result)
(I) Converts text to capital letters
(II) Removes extra spaces from text
(III) Joins two or more text strings
(IV) Capitalises the first letter of each word
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(I), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)
Why:
(A) UPPER("ram") → RAM (I).
(B) TRIM removes leading, trailing and repeated spaces (II).
(C) CONCATENATE joins strings, such as first and last names (III).
(D) PROPER("ram lal") → Ram Lal (IV).
Why not the others: (A) swaps UPPER and TRIM; (B) swaps TRIM and CONCATENATE; (C) swaps UPPER and PROPER.
Key point: Text functions clean master data such as customer names.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Payroll — HRA by IF on city type, then gross salary
questions.question: A payroll sheet computes HRA with =IF(D2="Metro",B2*50%,B2*40%). An employee's basic pay (B2) is ₹30,000, she works in a non-metro city (D2 = Non-metro), and her DA is 20% of basic pay. Her gross salary (basic + DA + HRA) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹48,000
Step 1: D2 is not "Metro" → HRA = ₹30,000 × 40% = ₹12,000
Step 2: DA = 20% × ₹30,000 = ₹6,000
Step 3: Gross = 30,000 + 6,000 + 12,000 = ₹48,000
Common mistake: Applying the metro rate (₹15,000) gives ₹51,000 (A). Leaving out HRA gives ₹42,000 (B). Basic + DA only gives ₹36,000 (D).

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Cell references — absolute, relative and mixed
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about cell references when a formula is copied:
(A) $A$1 does not change.
(B) A1 changes relative to the new position.
(C) $A1 keeps the column fixed.
(D) A$1 keeps the column fixed.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: A $ sign locks whatever follows it. $A$1 locks both (A); A1 locks nothing (B); $A1 locks the column (C).
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — in A$1 the $ is before the row number, so it is the ROW that stays fixed while the column can change. Options (A), (C) and (D) include it.
Key point: $ before the letter → column fixed; $ before the number → row fixed.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Loan schedule — balance outstanding with equal principal repayments
questions.question: A loan of ₹3,00,000 is repaid in 5 equal annual principal instalments, with interest paid separately. The loan balance outstanding at the end of the second year is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹1,80,000
Step 1: Annual principal instalment = ₹3,00,000 ÷ 5 = ₹60,000
Step 2: Repaid in two years = ₹1,20,000
Step 3: Outstanding = ₹3,00,000 − ₹1,20,000 = ₹1,80,000
Common mistake: ₹2,40,000 (A) is the balance after ONE year. ₹60,000 (B) is one instalment. ₹1,20,000 (C) is the amount repaid.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Spreadsheet file format
questions.question: A workbook saved in the standard format of a modern spreadsheet application such as MS Excel has the file extension:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) .xlsx
Why: .xlsx is the default workbook format of modern spreadsheet software; it stores multiple worksheets, formulas and formatting.
Why not the others:
(A) .docx is a word-processing document.
(C) .pptx is a presentation.
(D) .txt is plain text with no formulas.
Key point: Know the file type you are sharing — a CSV or TXT file loses formulas.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Charts — choosing a chart for composition
questions.question: To show what share each head (rent, salaries, power, others) forms of a firm's total expenses for one year, the most suitable chart is a:
options: C) Bar chart of yearly totals
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Pie chart
Why: A pie chart shows parts of a single whole, with each slice representing that head's share of the total.
Why not the others:
(A) Line charts show trends over time.
(B) Scatter charts show relationships between two variables.
(C) Yearly totals do not show the composition within one year.
Key point: Part-of-whole → pie; trend → line; comparison → bar or column.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Electronic spreadsheet — LEN
questions.question: The formula =LEN("Ledger 2026") returns:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 11
Why: LEN counts every character, including spaces: 'Ledger' (6) + space (1) + '2026' (4) = 11.
Why not the others:
(A) 10 forgets the space.
(B) 6 counts only 'Ledger'.
(D) 4 counts only '2026'.
Key point: LEN is used to check codes of fixed length, such as GSTINs or PAN numbers.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Electronic spreadsheet — IF with OR
questions.question: An allowance sheet uses =IF(OR(B2>60,C2="Manager"),"Eligible","Not eligible"). For an employee with B2 = 45 (age) and C2 = Manager, the formula returns:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Eligible
Why: OR returns TRUE if ANY condition is true. B2 > 60 is FALSE, but C2 = "Manager" is TRUE, so OR is TRUE and IF returns "Eligible".
Why not the others:
(A) would need both conditions to be false (or AND in place of OR).
(C) IF returns the specified text, not TRUE.
(D) The formula is valid.
Key point: AND → all conditions true; OR → at least one true.
